physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.prompt: A warehouse worker is booked for a 15-minute moist hot pack to the low back after the PT already screened the skin. How should the aide wrap and position the hydrocollator pack?

options.a: Use several terry layers, start the ordered timer, and rest the pack on the back rather than under the patient
options.b: Use one thin pillowcase so lumbar heat reaches the facet joints more quickly during the visit
options.c: Have the patient lie on the pack so body weight keeps the lumbar pack from sliding off
options.d: Leave the pack in place 45 minutes because the patient asked today for a deeper heating effect on the lumbar area

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.explanation: Aides set up moist heat as trained and as the PT/PTA ordered: intact skin, enough terry layers (commonly 6–8), a 15–20 minute timer, and the pack on top of the body. Compression from lying on a pack traps heat and is a classic burn setup. Extending time or stripping layers to “go deeper” is a clinician decision the aide does not make.

distractorExplanations.b: One thin pillowcase is far too little insulation; it raises burn risk instead of producing a useful deeper effect.
distractorExplanations.c: Lying on a hot pack compresses the layers and traps heat against the skin, a frequent cause of burns.
distractorExplanations.d: Typical moist-heat time is about 15–20 minutes; 45 minutes is a burn risk and is not an aide-chosen dose change.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.prompt: After a same-day ankle sprain, the PTA asks the aide to apply a clinic cold pack to the lateral ankle for 15 minutes. Which setup matches usual cryotherapy assist?

options.a: Place a thin cloth barrier, start the ordered timer, and check the skin during the hold
options.b: Put the gel pack on bare skin for 45 minutes so swelling drops faster before gait practice
options.c: Apply the pack over an area the patient cannot feel, because numbness means the ice is working
options.d: Start the cold pack first and wait until after the session for the PTA to look at the swelling

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.explanation: Aides may apply cold packs when directed: a barrier, the ordered time (often about 10–20 minutes), and skin checks. Direct ice for 45 minutes risks frostbite or nerve injury. Impaired sensation is a reason to stop and get the clinician, not a reason to proceed. Assessment of the injury stays with the PT/PTA.

distractorExplanations.b: Forty-five minutes on bare skin is far beyond a typical ice-pack window and can injure skin and superficial nerves.
distractorExplanations.c: Poor sensation is a cryotherapy precaution; the patient cannot report early frostbite or nerve-irritation signs.
distractorExplanations.d: The clinician assesses before treatment; an aide does not start cryotherapy ahead of that look.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.prompt: The PT is treating another patient two rooms away and called for therapeutic ultrasound to a rotator-cuff tendon. The aide has gel and the unit ready. Who sets frequency, intensity, and duty cycle?

options.a: The licensed PT or PTA sets and changes those parameters for this visit
options.b: The aide copies last Tuesday’s printout because the shoulder looked the same then
options.c: The aide switches the unit to 3 MHz so the beam will reach deeper cuff fibers today
options.d: The patient chooses a comfortable intensity and the aide locks those numbers in

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.explanation: Therapeutic ultrasound is a skilled modality. Aides may prepare the room, gel, and machine, but frequency, intensity, duty cycle, and treatment area are set and adjusted only by the PT or PTA. Copying an old card, reversing 1 MHz vs 3 MHz, or letting the patient pick dose is still the aide choosing parameters.

distractorExplanations.b: Reusing last session’s numbers is still the aide selecting dose; the clinician sets parameters each visit.
distractorExplanations.c: 3 MHz is more superficial and 1 MHz is deeper; aides do not change frequency to chase depth.
distractorExplanations.d: Comfort can be reported to the clinician, but the patient does not prescribe ultrasound dose.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.prompt: A PTA marked two electrode sites on a runner’s vastus medialis and asked the aide to attach pre-gelled pads after a skin check. Where do the pads go?

options.a: On the two marked sites after confirming the skin is intact and clean
options.b: Wherever the runner points as the most painful spot, even if that is a new site
options.c: One pad on each anterior shoulder so current can travel across the chest wall
options.d: Over the anterior neck if the runner also mentions tight cervical muscles today

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.explanation: Electrical stimulation placement is a skilled order. After a skin check, the aide applies pads only where the PT/PTA specified. Patient pointing can land pads on wounds, implants, or other contraindicated sites. Current across the thorax or over the anterior neck (carotid sinus) is unsafe.

distractorExplanations.b: Pain-point placement is a clinical judgment; following the patient’s finger can put pads on contraindicated tissue.
distractorExplanations.c: Transthoracic current is contraindicated because it can interfere with heart rhythm.
distractorExplanations.d: Anterior-neck stimulation over the carotid sinus is a contraindicated e-stim site.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.prompt: A cervical traction table is booked after the PT’s evaluation. The aide is asked to get the harness and table ready while the PT finishes a note. What is the aide’s role on dose?

options.a: Raise pounds a little from last visit so the patient feels a stronger stretch today
options.b: Prep the harness, table, and comfort items; the PT or PTA enters the pull and time
options.c: Start the pull while the patient dozes if the schedule is tight and the hallway is quiet
options.d: Hook every neck-pain arrival to the same poundage because the protocol sheet is in the drawer

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.explanation: Aides may position the table, harness, and pillows as trained. Traction force, angle, hold/rest, and duration are skilled parameters the PT/PTA sets and monitors. Increasing pounds, running traction unattended, or auto-applying a stock neck protocol is practicing outside aide scope.

distractorExplanations.a: Pounds are a skilled dose; an aide does not progress traction because the patient wants a stronger stretch.
distractorExplanations.c: Traction is monitored by the licensed clinician; an unattended sleeping patient is not a safe setup.
distractorExplanations.d: Neck pain is not an automatic traction order; the evaluating PT decides whether traction is even indicated.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.prompt: An older adult with hand osteoarthritis is scheduled for paraffin. At the sink the aide sees a fresh paper-cut that is still oozing on the index finger. What should the aide do?

options.a: Dip the hand anyway because stiffness from arthritis is the usual reason for paraffin
options.b: Hold the dip, cover nothing with wax, and get the PT or PTA before the unit is used
options.c: Proceed because the unit is already at its ordinary working temperature this afternoon
options.d: Dip only the other fingers and tell the patient the cut will seal under the wax layers

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.explanation: Open skin is a contraindication for paraffin: wax can burn damaged tissue and the communal bath is an infection risk. The aide stops, does not improvise a partial dip, and flags the licensed clinician. Arthritis stiffness and a unit at normal temperature are indications or equipment-ready signs, not permission to ignore a wound.

distractorExplanations.a: Arthritic stiffness is a common indication, but an open cut overrides that and must be reported first.
distractorExplanations.c: A unit at about 125–127 °F is ready for intact skin; temperature does not make an open wound safe.
distractorExplanations.d: Sealing a cut under wax hides a contraindication and still contaminates the bath.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.prompt: Between a morning interferential session and the next patient, the aide is turning over the treatment table. What cleaning step belongs in that turnover?

options.a: Wipe the unit and straps with a dry towel so they look ready for the next arrival
options.b: Disinfect surfaces, straps, and reusable electrodes with the clinic-approved product
options.c: Skip straps until Friday’s deep clean and only change the pillowcase now
options.d: Disinfect the machine once at closing because the same unit is used all afternoon

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.explanation: Shared modality hardware is a fomite. Aides clean between patients with the product the manufacturer and clinic policy allow on that unit, including straps and reusable electrodes. A dry wipe is not disinfection. End-of-day or weekly cleaning leaves the next patient exposed.

distractorExplanations.a: A dry towel may remove lint but does not disinfect skin-contact surfaces between patients.
distractorExplanations.c: Straps and belts touch skin; they are cleaned between patients, not parked until a weekly wipe.
distractorExplanations.d: Once-daily disinfection is too infrequent for equipment that contacts successive patients.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.prompt: Three minutes into a thoracic hot pack, a clinic patient says, “This is burning, not just warm.” The PT is in the next booth. What should the aide do first?

options.a: Add two more towels and keep the pack on so the visit stays on the 15-minute clock
options.b: Remove the pack at once, inspect what you can see, and get the PT to the booth
options.c: Ask the patient to wait two minutes because packs often feel hottest at the start
options.d: Walk to the hydrocollator and turn the thermostat down for whoever is treated after lunch

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.explanation: A burn complaint stops heat immediately. The aide removes the pack, does not keep treating through pain, and summons the PT/PTA for a skin check and next steps. Adding layers while the pack stays on, waiting it out, or adjusting the tank first delays care and can deepen a burn.

distractorExplanations.a: A burning report ends the modality; extra towels with the pack still on delay a skin check.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting for the pack to “settle” can turn a superficial burn into a deeper injury.
distractorExplanations.d: Tank temperature can be reviewed later; the first action is removing the pack and alerting the clinician.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.prompt: The PTA asked the aide to perform ice massage to a small lateral-epicondyle area after demonstrating the stroke. Midway, the patient says the skin feels dead and the area looks blotchy-white. What should the aide do?

options.a: Continue because cold, then burn, then ache are the usual stages before numbness
options.b: Stop at the two-minute mark regardless of skin, because that is a standard ice-massage cap
options.c: Stop the ice, protect the skin, and get the PTA because sensation and color have changed
options.d: Keep going while the skin is only pink, treating mild redness as proof the ice is safe

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.explanation: Expected ice-massage stages are cold, burn, ache, then numbness, with mild pinkness common. Loss of sensation plus blotchy or white skin is a stop sign: end the ice, protect the area, and notify the clinician. Two minutes is not a universal stop rule, and “keep going through warning signs” is unsafe.

distractorExplanations.a: Cold-burn-ache can be expected, but “dead” feeling with blotchy-white skin is past those stages and is a stop.
distractorExplanations.b: Ice massage is often about 5–10 minutes or until numbness; a hard two-minute cut is not the safety rule here.
distractorExplanations.d: Mild pink can be normal; white, mottled, or wheal-like skin with no feeling is a reason to stop.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.prompt: A patient finishing a directed hot pack asks the aide to “just add 10 minutes of ultrasound too—the PT did that last month.” The PT is in a team meeting. What should the aide do?

options.a: Start ultrasound at last month’s settings so the patient does not lose the extra modality
options.b: Agree to the extra ultrasound if the patient signs a note that it was requested, not ordered
options.c: Keep today's order, decline extra ultrasound, and get the PT or PTA first
options.d: Offer a TENS trial from a spare clinic unit because that is a similar electrical treatment

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.explanation: Aides do not independently prescribe or add skilled modalities. A request based on an old visit is not a current order. The aide stays with what was directed this session and finds the PT/PTA. Substituting TENS or running ultrasound from memory is still unlicensed practice.

distractorExplanations.a: Last month’s ultrasound is not today’s order; starting it is independent delivery of a skilled modality.
distractorExplanations.b: A patient signature does not create an order or expand aide scope.
distractorExplanations.d: TENS is a different modality with its own parameters and indications; swapping it in is still prescribing.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.prompt: A hydrocollator pack comes out dripping and the aide is wrapping it for a PT-ordered lumbar heat. What insulation choice is appropriate?

options.a: Slide the wet pack into one thin pillowcase so it can go on the table immediately
options.b: Wrap it in plastic film only so moisture stays in and heat lasts through the full 20-minute hold
options.c: Blot excess water, then use enough dry terry layers so the pack is not dripping on skin
options.d: Keep the dripping towel against the back because wet heat is supposed to feel hotter

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.explanation: Hydrocollator packs need enough dry terry insulation; a dripping pack conducts heat too fast and burns. Aides blot extra water and layer as trained. A single pillowcase, plastic wrap, or a soaked towel against skin are common burn setups, not acceptable shortcuts.

distractorExplanations.a: One pillowcase is not enough insulation, especially with a wet pack still dripping.
distractorExplanations.b: Plastic wrap traps heat and moisture against skin and does not replace terry layers.
distractorExplanations.d: A dripping-wet towel conducts heat rapidly and is a frequent cause of moist-heat burns.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.prompt: A patient brings a personal TENS unit from home and asks the aide to turn intensity up because clinic pain is worse than last night. Clinic policy lets aides help with pad adhesion only. What should the aide do?

options.a: Increase intensity two clicks because the patient owns the device and knows the usual feeling
options.b: Use the home unit on the next patient when the clinic stim machine is already busy
options.c: Leave the program as set, help with pads per policy, and get the PT for changes
options.d: Unplug the clinic interferential unit and treat from the home TENS because both are electrical

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.explanation: Home TENS belongs to that patient and stays within clinic policy and the PT’s instructions. Aides do not reprogram intensity, substitute a personal unit for ordered clinic e-stim, or share one patient’s device. Parameter changes go to the licensed clinician.

distractorExplanations.a: Raising intensity is a parameter change; ownership of the unit does not give the aide that authority.
distractorExplanations.b: A personal device is not shared; using it on others is an infection-control and privacy failure.
distractorExplanations.d: A home TENS unit does not replace clinic e-stim the PT ordered for this visit.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.prompt: The aide set up a cold pack and stayed in the booth while the PTA ran the rest of the session. How should the aide’s note read?

options.a: Write that the aide progressed the plan of care because swelling looked improved at the end
options.b: Leave the reddened skin off the note so the chart does not look like a complication occurred
options.c: Copy yesterday’s identical heat note even though today was ice, to keep the flow sheet tidy
options.d: Record what the aide set up, the time, and that the PTA directed and monitored the modality

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.explanation: Aide documentation is factual assist: what was prepared, time, patient report, and who directed the skilled portion. Aides do not claim they changed the plan of care, hide skin changes, or copy a prior note that does not match today’s modality. Honest assist notes protect the patient and the license holder.

distractorExplanations.a: Progressing the plan of care is a PT function; an aide must not chart skilled decision-making they did not do.
distractorExplanations.b: Omitting a skin change hides a possible burn or cold injury and falsifies the record.
distractorExplanations.c: Copying yesterday’s heat note for today’s ice is inaccurate charting.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.prompt: A whirlpool is ordered at a stated temperature for a foot wound-care visit. The tank thermometer reads several degrees hotter than the order. What should the aide do?

options.a: Start the soak anyway because warmer water feels better to most patients with stiff feet
options.b: Add extra hot water until the patient says it matches a home bath they like
options.c: Skip the thermometer and time the soak by how red the skin looks after five minutes
options.d: Hold the whirlpool and have the PT or PTA correct the temperature before soaking

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.explanation: Whirlpool temperature is part of the skilled order. If the tank does not match, the aide holds treatment and gets the PT/PTA. Patient preference, “a little hotter feels better,” or judging dose by skin color are not substitutes for the ordered temperature and can burn compromised skin.

distractorExplanations.a: Comfort is not a reason to exceed the ordered temperature, especially on a wound.
distractorExplanations.b: Home-bath preference does not authorize the aide to retitrate hydrotherapy heat.
distractorExplanations.c: Skin redness is a late burn sign, not a safe way to set or confirm whirlpool temperature.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.prompt: The supervising PT left the building for a school visit. A follow-up patient is on the board for ultrasound that the PT usually delivers. The front desk asks the aide to “just run it so we do not cancel.” What should the aide do?

options.a: Deliver the ultrasound alone using the card from the last visit so the slot is not wasted
options.b: Have the PTA who is off-site on lunch text a thumbs-up, then start the unit
options.c: Let the patient self-treat with the sound head while the aide watches from the doorway
options.d: Hold ultrasound until a PT or PTA is on site to direct it; follow notify-and-reschedule steps

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-mo.explanation: PT aides are unlicensed assistive personnel. They do not independently deliver skilled ultrasound, even with an old parameter card, a remote text, or the patient holding the head. When no PT/PTA is present to direct the modality, the aide does not start it and follows clinic procedure to notify and reschedule.

distractorExplanations.a: Running ultrasound with the PT off-site is independent skilled treatment, outside aide scope.
distractorExplanations.b: A text from someone who is not on site is not in-person direction or supervision of a skilled modality.
distractorExplanations.c: Patient self-application still leaves an ordered skilled modality unsupervised; the aide must not start it.
